examples: Revenue acceleration that is accompanied by rising gross margins signals pricing power and operating leverage, which the market recognizes only gradually.
Accelerating sales matter most for firms that the market values cheaply relative to revenue, because the acceleration is then least reflected in the price.
groups.why: Growth acceleration says nothing about value discount or quality.

groups.area: Accounting losses that hide cash coverage
examples: Loss-making firms whose cash coverage of liabilities is improving are being penalized for past accounting losses, and the improvement is not yet reflected in price.
Firms that report a loss but would be profitable after adding back R&D, and that also generate cash relative to liabilities, are undervalued relative to their true earning power.
groups.why: Hidden cash coverage and undervaluation fit discount tenet; losses weak on quality.

groups.area: Accrual spike in an issuance year
examples: Within an industry, firms with the largest year-over-year accrual increases that also issue securities are the most likely to be selling overvalued equity or debt.
Firms whose accruals jump in the same year they issue equity or debt are inflating earnings ahead of security sales, so they should underperform the following month.
groups.why: Avoiding accrual inflators who issue securities fits management alignment and quality.

examples: Firms that are expensive relative to their industry peers on book value and report high accruals (earnings not backed by operating cash) are overpriced glamour stocks, so their subsequent returns are low.

Within each industry, firms that are expensive on market-to-book and also report high accruals (earnings running ahead of cash) are overpriced glamour stocks, and their returns underperform over the next month.
groups.why: Avoids expensive stocks with poor earnings quality; discount and quality tenets.

examples: Stocks combining high accruals with a thin book-equity cushion relative to peers are close to covenant or distress thresholds, and their inflated earnings are likely to be marked down.
Accruals that persist over three years at highly leveraged firms indicate a managed earnings path that cannot be sustained, and the reversal hits stocks with the least balance-sheet room.
groups.why: Avoids leveraged low-quality earnings; business quality criteria.

examples: Within each industry, firms whose operating cash flow exceeds earnings are less exposed to accrual reversal, and this quality matters most when the market is paying up for sales growth.
groups.why: Cash-backed earnings support quality; growth-premium focus is not value.

examples: Non-cash working capital build scaled by sales in fast-growing firms reflects receivables and inventory that are added to support growth and tend to unwind, reducing later earnings and returns.
Accruals that persist over three years in growing firms are a sign of a sustained gap between reported and realized earnings, which compounds into a larger later correction than a one-year spike.
groups.why: Avoids low-quality accruals; quality tenet, but growth firms not value-specific.

examples: Abrupt jumps in accruals that coincide with abrupt jumps in net external financing indicate a new earnings-and-capital push, which the market underreacts to until results reverse.
Accruals funded by new debt relative to the firm's existing capital structure signal greater financial distress risk and a higher chance of earnings manipulation to preserve credit access.
groups.why: Avoids issuers with accrual inflation; shareholder alignment and quality.

examples: Within an industry, firms that accrue more earnings while their effective tax rate compresses are booking profits that are less tax-supported, which tends to precede lower returns.

Accruals that persistently outpace the decline in tax burden over several years indicate a systematic book-tax wedge that is more likely to reflect aggressive reporting than a single transitory event.
groups.why: Avoids aggressive reporting; quality tenet supports.

groups.area: Accruals with an external funding gap

groups.why: Buys high accruals with external financing; contradicts quality and alignment.

groups.area: Accruals with an external funding gap
examples: A sudden jump in accruals that coincides with heavy new issuance signals that management is manufacturing reported earnings to support a capital raise, which precedes low returns.
Firms whose accrual ratio is unstable over five years and whose smoothed financing gap is large are managing earnings opportunistically with outside capital, which predicts low future returns.
groups.why: Avoids earnings manipulation and issuance; management alignment and quality.

examples: Smoothed accruals that stay high while retained earnings decline in the trend sense point to firms where reported earnings keep outrunning cash while equity is being depleted, a combination the market underreacts to.
groups.why: Buys eroding equity with high accruals; quality criteria.

examples: A sharp acceleration in accrual buildup alongside shrinking retained earnings marks a deteriorating earnings trajectory that investors extrapolate, producing subsequent underperformance.
Accruals that accumulate over several years while retained earnings repeatedly decline signal persistent earnings overstatement and balance-sheet stress, which the market prices only gradually.
groups.why: Avoids overstated earnings and balance-sheet stress; quality criteria.

groups.why: Organic innovation suggests disciplined capital allocation; no valuation.

examples: The fraction of total intangible investment that is bought rather than built predicts lower subsequent returns.
A sharp rise in acquisition spending relative to assets signals management overreach, and the market only partly prices the deals when they are announced.
groups.why: Avoids acquisition overreach; owner-minded capital allocation.

examples: Firms whose working capital and retained earnings relative to assets are rising are moving away from distress, and the market reacts to this improvement with a lag.
Firms with persistently high pre-tax earning power relative to assets, and low volatility in that power, carry less distress risk and are underpriced for their stability.
groups.why: Lower distress supports business quality; no valuation link.

examples: The asset-renewal premium is concentrated in tangible-asset firms, where the stock of old fixed capital is economically large and depreciation is a meaningful measure of its aging.
Firms that have spent less than their depreciation for several consecutive years accumulate an asset-age backlog, and the eventual catch-up spending lifts returns as the backlog is worked off.
groups.why: Asset age says little about value or quality.

examples: Asset expansion is most value-destructive when it is not backed by current profitability, so firms that grow assets while earning low returns on assets underperform.
When the balance sheet expands faster than revenue, capital is being added without a matching increase in sales, a sign of unproductive investment that predicts low future returns.
groups.why: Avoids empire building; owner-like capital allocation discipline.

examples: A firm whose worst annual PP&E contraction over the past three years is severe is undergoing a multi-year restructuring episode, and the market under-rewards the persistence of the asset-shedding process.

Restructuring is a multi-year process, so firms that have shrunk their tangible asset intensity in several of the last five years are executing a sustained transition that the market prices only gradually.
groups.why: Restructuring episodes not addressed by tenets.

examples: Firms with more physical collateral and fewer intangible assets have more recoverable value in liquidation, which lowers their distress risk and expected return premium.
Industry-relative tangibility matters most for firms that already carry meaningful debt, because collateral is only priced as a distress buffer when it supports borrowing.
groups.why: Tangible collateral aids downside; not about valuation.

groups.area: Book equity understated by expensed R&D
examples: Firms that are rapidly building their hidden knowledge stock relative to assets are investing ahead of earnings, and the market under-reacts to this growth in unrecorded capital.

Adding the five-year R&D stock back to book equity gives a corrected book-to-market ratio, and within-industry value on this corrected measure predicts returns better than conventional book-to-market.
groups.why: Value on corrected book plus investment; discount to intrinsic value.

examples: Firms that pay a high share of pre-tax income in taxes, both relative to their industry and relative to their own five-year history, have earnings that are better backed by cash and should earn higher future returns.

When the effective tax rate falls sharply year on year while pre-tax income holds up, earnings are being lifted by tax benefits, such as valuation allowance releases or credits, which are non-recurring; stocks where the
groups.why: Cash-backed earnings support quality; no valuation.

examples: Firms whose pre-tax income far exceeds the tax implied by a 21% statutory rate, scaled by assets and ranked within industry, report earnings that are less likely to persist, so future returns are lower.

A widening book-tax gap, meaning earnings are rising faster than cash tax obligations, signals that reported profit growth is being driven by a temporary wedge that will reverse, which lowers subsequent returns.
groups.why: Avoids non-persistent earnings; business quality criteria.

examples: Cheap book value earns a premium only when the firm is currently profitable; book-to-market among loss-making firms mostly reflects distress rather than mispricing.
Book-to-market predicts returns mainly among stocks that have recently fallen, because those are the ones where price has moved away from accounting value and a rebound is most likely.
groups.why: Buys cheap book value; discount to intrinsic value.

examples: Book-to-market predicts returns only among firms whose earnings are cash-backed (negative total accruals), while cheap firms with positive accruals are value traps.
Within each industry, the cheapest firms with the cleanest accruals are the ones where the valuation discount reflects mispricing rather than a justified fundamental gap.
groups.why: Cheap with clean accruals; discount plus quality.

examples: Firms that are cheap on book-to-market and are not absorbing capital into working capital earn higher subsequent returns than cheap firms that are growing working capital.
Cheap firms whose working-capital investment is stable and predictable are managed with discipline, and their low valuations reflect mispricing rather than deteriorating operations.
groups.why: Cheap with disciplined operations; discount plus quality.

examples: The weakest buyback intensity over the past three years captures firms that never paused repurchases even in bad years, which signals a payout floor that management protects.
Firms that are net shrinkers, repurchasing more stock than they issue, in most of the last five years have a disciplined equity-capital policy that avoids the dilution anomaly.
groups.why: Consistent buybacks show owner-aligned management.

examples: Buybacks started out of internally generated free cash flow, rather than borrowed money, are more likely to be sustainable and to reflect genuine confidence in the business.
Buyback initiations made after a year of share-price weakness are a stronger undervaluation signal, because management is responding to a price decline it views as excessive.
groups.why: Buybacks funded from FCF after weakness; alignment and undervaluation.

examples: Repurchase intensity predicts high next-month returns only when reported earnings are backed by operating cash flow, so buybacks are informative only in the cash-backed regime.
Persistent multi-year repurchases relative to market value, held by firms with consistently low accruals over three years, signal management's sustained confidence that the stock is cheap.
groups.why: Buybacks with cash-backed earnings; alignment and quality.

examples: Stocks that combine rapid two-year capex growth with low operating profitability on assets are over-investing into poor returns and will underperform.
Firms whose capex-to-assets ratio has climbed far above its own five-year low are in an extended buildup phase whose returns are likely to disappoint.
groups.why: Avoids over-investment into poor returns; capital allocation discipline.

examples: Firms with heavy capital per dollar of sales and with unstable tangibility profiles face greater operating and financing uncertainty, which investors demand compensation for.
Stocks that are both asset-heavy and short of liquid cash bear more funding and redeployment risk, and this combination should earn higher expected returns than tangibility alone.
groups.why: Risk-premium capital intensity; tenets silent.

examples: Lean working capital only translates into durable excess returns for firms with high gross margins, because only those firms have the pricing power that makes fast collection and low inventory a sign of demand strength r
groups.why: Lean working capital with margins signals quality.

examples: Firms with a long cash conversion cycle relative to their industry peers tie up more working capital per dollar of sales and earn lower subsequent returns.
Firms whose receivable and inventory intensities fluctuate sharply over five years have unstable operations and demand, which investors discount, leading to lower future returns.
groups.why: Avoiding tied-up capital and unstable operations supports quality.

groups.area: Cash coverage of liabilities at fragile firms
examples: Firms whose minimum operating-cash-flow-to-liabilities ratio over the past three years remains high are durably solvent, and this durability is priced most when leverage is high.
For levered firms (liabilities above half of assets), an improving trend in cash coverage of liabilities signals deleveraging capacity and reduced distress, which the market extrapolates too slowly.
groups.why: Durable solvency supports business quality.

groups.area: Cash coverage of liabilities at fragile firms
examples: Levered firms whose cash coverage fluctuates little over five years have predictable debt-servicing capacity, and investors who price the average rather than the volatility of coverage leave a premium on the steady names

Levered firms reporting earnings well above operating cash flow carry accrual-driven profits that tend to reverse, so the market is too generous to their reported earnings; the cash-rich, levered side of the accrual dist
groups.why: Avoids accrual-driven profits at levered firms; quality.

examples: The return premium on cash is concentrated in firms whose operating cash flow is weak, because for them cash is the only buffer against funding shortfalls.
The minimum cash-to-assets ratio over the past five years, rather than the current level, captures a structural liquidity reserve that the firm never draws down.
groups.why: Liquidity buffer supports quality; weak on valuation.

examples: Share shrink is only a quality signal when it is paid for out of operating cash; buybacks funded by debt or asset sales do not create owner value.
A falling share count is high quality when leverage is not rising, because it indicates equity shrink that is not a leveraged recapitalization that raises financial risk.
groups.why: Cash-funded buybacks without leverage; owner alignment.

examples: A firm whose cash coverage of recent cumulative R&D has been rising steadily is building a durable runway that funds future research without dilution.
Research funded from net cash (cash minus long-term debt) rather than borrowed money reflects a firm that can afford its innovation pipeline without refinancing risk.
groups.why: Funded R&D supports quality; no valuation.

examples: A cash-flow surplus over net income that persists across three fiscal years reflects durable earnings conservatism, which the market prices with a lag.
A large cash-earnings gap is more valuable when it is stable, because volatile wedges reflect noisy timing of accruals and cash receipts that the market correctly discounts.
groups.why: Cash exceeding earnings supports earnings quality.

examples: A cash-minus-earnings gap that is stable over five years indicates consistently conservative accounting, while a gap that swings sharply signals timing manipulation or noisy accruals. The chosen fifth should be firms wit
groups.why: Stable cash-earnings gap supports quality.

groups.area: Cash yield with a current-ratio trough
examples: A firm's cash-generating strength is only as credible as its weakest recent liquidity position, so the signal should be limited by the weaker of the two channels rather than their average.

Stocks with high operating cash yield earn higher subsequent returns, but only when the firm's liquidity never fell far in its recent history, so the cash yield is less likely to be a distressed or value trap.
groups.why: Cash yield cheap with liquidity; discount plus quality.

examples: Firms whose cash-minus-earnings gap is widening relative to assets are improving their earnings quality and the market reacts with a lag as the improvement shows up in later reported results.
A firm whose worst cash-minus-earnings gap over three years is still positive has persistently cash-backed earnings, which the market underprices relative to firms with one-off cash surpluses.
groups.why: Cash-backed earnings quality; no valuation.

examples: Gross profitability is more valuable when it is not accompanied by rapid expansion of non-cash current assets, so firms with high gross profit and low working-capital build-up outperform.
Firms whose cash-adjusted gross profitability has been steadily rising over five years, rather than merely being high, are early in a margin-expansion cycle that the market extrapolates too slowly.
groups.why: Profitability with cash backing supports quality.

examples: Cash operating profit yield on market value identifies undervalued firms, and this yield is most informative when compared within industries.
Firms whose operating profit is backed by cash after working-capital build-up earn higher subsequent returns, and this holds relative to industry peers.
groups.why: Cash profit yield on market value; cheap and quality.

examples: When top-line growth runs ahead of growth in cash-based operating profitability, the firm is buying revenue with receivables, inventory, or price concessions that do not convert to cash, and such firms underperform as th
groups.why: Avoids revenue not converting to cash; quality.

groups.area: Cash-flow or EBITDA yield with a cash floor
examples: Cheap firms whose cash generation on assets is trending upward are early-stage recoveries that the market has not yet priced, whereas cheap firms with deteriorating cash trends are continuing to decay.

Cheap firms whose operating cash flow per dollar of assets has been stable over five years are healthy value stocks, while cheap firms with erratic cash generation are more likely to be distressed traps.
groups.why: Cheap with stable cash generation; discount plus quality.

examples: Firms whose cash yield has stayed above a floor over five years carry durable cash generation that the market discounts as temporary.
Stocks that are cheap on cash flow and whose cash returns on assets are improving are undervalued before the market incorporates the operating turnaround.
groups.why: Cash-flow cheapness; discount to intrinsic value.

examples: A firm that repeatedly retires shares from cash over several years is signaling durable excess cash generation, which the market tends to discount when it views buybacks as one-off or cyclical.
Repurchases that are not financed by net new equity or net new debt signal that management is returning surplus internal cash, and the market under-reacts to that signal relative to its market value.
groups.why: Cash-funded buybacks relative to value; alignment and cheapness.

examples: Loss-making firms that still generate strong operating cash flow relative to assets are early-stage turnarounds, and the market extrapolates the accounting loss too far.
Within industries, loss-making firms with the highest operating cash flow relative to assets have the most real operating capacity, so the market's pessimism about their reported losses is overdone.
groups.why: Cash generation beneath losses may be mispriced; losses weaken quality.

examples: Buybacks carry the undervaluation signal only when the firm is a net cash holder, because a levered firm repurchasing shares is more likely funding payouts with debt than signaling mispricing.
Stocks trading near their cash balance that have net repurchased shares over the last three years are being bought back by managers who view the equity as undervalued relative to the cash backing it.
groups.why: Cheap cash-rich buyers; discount and owner alignment.

groups.area: Cash-rich cheap firms that are not spending
examples: Cash-rich firms whose capex-to-sales has been declining over five years are shrinking their reinvestment while holding cash, and the market under-prices the resulting payout capacity.

Cheap cash-rich firms predict returns only when they have been persistently under-investing over the last three years. A cash-to-market-value rank is therefore gated by a three-year low-capex condition.
groups.why: Cheap cash-rich with capital discipline.

groups.area: Cheap after a fall with low accruals
examples: A stock is over-sold only when it has fallen, trades cheap on operating cash flow, and has low accruals, so all three conditions must hold at the same time.
Stocks that are cheap on book value and have fallen over the long run, while showing no working-capital accrual build, are over-sold relative to their balance-sheet value.
groups.why: Cheap, oversold, clean accruals; discount plus quality.

groups.area: Cheap because losing money: the value trap
examples: Firms that are cheap on book-to-market and currently report net losses are priced low because the market expects continued distress, so their subsequent returns underperform.
Book-to-market cheapness combined with a history of repeated net losses over five years signals a structural value trap, where low prices persist because earnings power has not recovered.
groups.why: Avoids value traps from persistent losses; quality criteria.

groups.area: Cheap firms borrowing to pay dividends
examples: Among high book-to-market firms, those that simultaneously pay large dividends and fund them with net new debt are overvalued relative to their cash-generating ability, so they underperform.

High dividend yield combined with rising long-term leverage is a "yield trap": the dividend is maintained by adding debt, and the high yield reflects a low price that the market expects to fall further.
groups.why: Avoids debt-funded dividends; prudent capital allocation.

groups.area: Cheap firms that pay real taxes
examples: Cheap stocks whose tax payments have stayed above a floor for five years have durable taxable profits, so their earnings yield is more likely to persist and be recognized by the market over the next year.

Cheap firms whose tax payments are stable over time are less likely to be in a volatile earnings cycle, so their low valuation reflects a mispriced steady income stream rather than a cyclical peak or trough.
groups.why: Cheap with durable taxable profits; discount plus quality.

groups.area: Cheap firms with inventory piling up
examples: Stocks with high sales yield whose inventory intensity has never recently spiked offer value without a recent demand-shock overhang, so they should outperform cheap names carrying a recent inventory peak.

Book-to-market is only a value signal when inventory is not expanding, so the cheapest stocks that are not building inventory should outperform, while cheap stocks that are stockpiling are demoted to the middle of the ra
groups.why: Cheap without inventory build; discount plus quality.

groups.area: Cheap firms with inventory piling up
examples: A multi-year rise in inventory relative to sales, not a single-year spike, indicates a persistent demand shortfall that depresses future returns for value stocks.
Cheap stocks whose inventory is accumulating relative to the asset base are likely facing weakening demand that the market has not yet priced, so they underperform.
groups.why: Avoids cheap firms with inventory build; value-trap avoidance.

groups.area: Cheap firms with low asset growth
examples: Operating earnings yield predicts returns only for firms whose total assets are shrinking; among expanding firms, cheapness is a value trap.
Cheap firms whose assets are growing faster than their sales, so asset intensity is rising, underperform; cheap firms whose asset intensity is falling outperform.
groups.why: Cheap with disciplined asset growth.

examples: Stocks in sectors whose book-to-market sits well above the sector median are being priced at a whole-industry discount, and that discount closes as sector-level mispricing corrects.
Stocks rank high only when they are cheap on both book and operating earnings relative to industry peers, and this joint discount predicts higher returns than either discount alone.
groups.why: Cheap relative to industry; discount to value.

examples: Share count growth that outpaces sales growth is equity issuance that does not fund real expansion, and the market eventually penalizes it.
A sharp rise in this year's dilution relative to last year's signals a new financing need or opportunistic issuance window that the market has not yet priced.
groups.why: Avoids dilution; shareholder alignment.

examples: Cheap firms whose depreciation rate is rising year over year are reporting conservatively, so their book value and earnings are understated relative to a stable-depreciation peer.
Cheap firms where depreciation is a large share of operating costs have earnings understated by conservative depreciation, so their true operating profitability is higher than the market prices.
groups.why: Cheap with conservative accounting; discount plus quality.

examples: When long-term debt grows faster than book equity, the firm's capital structure is drifting toward leverage, and that drift is priced with a lag, producing underperformance.
Cumulative three-year net debt issuance scaled by equity market value captures persistent borrowing that drives mispricing, which is more durable than a single-year debt jump.
groups.why: Avoids leverage drift; prudent capital allocation.

examples: Firms whose short-term debt is large relative to their cash and recurring operating cash flow face a near-term funding gap, and this gap is slow to be priced.
When more than half of a firm's debt is due within a year, low liquidity turns a refinancing need into distress risk, and the market underprices this conditional exposure.
groups.why: Avoids refinancing-exposed firms; business quality.

examples: Sustained multi-year debt repayment, rather than a single-year move, signals a deliberate deleveraging policy that is rewarded when operating cash flow is steady.
The fraction of outstanding debt a firm retires in a year measures the intensity of its deleveraging, and this intensity is more credible when cash flow is steady.
groups.why: Deliberate deleveraging by steady firms; quality and prudence.

examples: Firms whose short-term debt has been rising relative to cash over five years are accumulating a refinancing wall that the market prices late, so their subsequent 12-month returns lag.
The size of short-term debt only matters for returns when cash does not cover it, so the market penalizes large short-term debt in firms whose cash falls short of the near-term claim.
groups.why: Avoids refinancing pressure; quality criteria.

examples: Firms that add debt faster than their asset base while earning little operating profit on assets are funding low-quality growth, and their subsequent returns are weak.
Within an industry, firms that add more net debt relative to assets while earning less than their peers are expanding on borrowed money at the expense of equity returns.
groups.why: Avoids debt-funded growth at weak earners; capital discipline.

examples: The damage from debt-funded payouts is largest when the firm already pays heavy interest, because borrowing to fund distributions compounds a cost burden that limits future flexibility.

Net debt issuance predicts low returns only when the firm is actually paying out more than its operating cash flow. Without that shortfall, new borrowing may be investment-driven and carry no mispricing.
groups.why: Avoids debt-funded payouts; owner-like prudence.

examples: A persistent multi-year accumulation of deferred tax liabilities, rather than a one-year blip, reflects a sustained gap between book and taxable income that markets underreact to.

A deferred tax balance that has built up steadily over three years reflects persistent gap between reported and taxable income, which is a durable forensic warning rather than a one-year timing effect.
groups.why: Avoids book-tax wedge warning; quality.

examples: Profitable firms whose depreciation rate swings year to year are frequently revising useful-life or salvage assumptions, a pattern associated with managing reported earnings that later reverses.
A multi-year downward drift in the depreciation rate, present only in firms with positive ROA, signals a sustained policy of extending asset lives to hold up reported profits, with later reversal.
groups.why: Avoids earnings managers; management quality.

examples: Earnings inflated by accruals that exceed cash flow, and that also carry a low tax burden, are the most likely to be overstated, and the overstatement reverses in subsequent returns.
Stocks whose depreciation-to-assets ratio fell this year while their industry-relative tax burden is low show overstated book earnings, and their returns are lower in the following month.
groups.why: Avoids overstated earnings; management quality.

examples: Stocks where depreciation policy has tightened and cash earnings exceed accounting earnings combine two independent signs of earnings that are not inflated by accounting choices.
Firms that raised their depreciation rate in several of the last three years have a persistent policy of conservative asset-life estimates, and this consistency is not priced into the stock.
groups.why: Conservative accounting by management; quality.

groups.area: Distance from the multi-year low in profits
examples: Firms that have climbed most of the way from the bottom of their five-year EBITDA-to-assets range, relative to their own history, are still priced as if they remain near the trough.
Firms whose operating profitability has risen well above its five-year trough are underpriced, because investors extrapolate the earlier depressed margins and under-update on the recovery.
groups.why: Recovering profits still priced low; some discount.

examples: Issuing more equity than close industry peers while carrying above-peer leverage signals that a firm is raising capital from a weak position, and these dilutive raises underperform.
Firms that issue equity in many of the last five years while carrying heavy debt are serial diluters that repeatedly fail to fund themselves internally, and their shares underperform.
groups.why: Avoids serial diluters; shareholder alignment.

examples: Firms that raise dividends in several of the last three years and trade cheaply within their industry are signaling durable cash-flow confidence that the market has not yet priced.
When a cheap firm's dividend yield expands year-over-year, the price has not caught up with a payout increase that reflects managerial confidence, so the stock should earn abnormal returns.
groups.why: Cheap with rising dividends; discount and alignment.

examples: Dividends started out of internally generated cash flow, not external equity issuance, are a durable commitment and predict higher subsequent returns.
Dividend changes are informative relative to industry peers, since payout norms differ across sectors, and firms that initiate when rivals do not stand out.
groups.why: Cash-funded dividends show owner orientation.

examples: Firms that have paid dividends in most of the last five years and are not accelerating capital spending form a stable, mature cash-return group whose returns are underpriced.
Cheap dividend payers become attractive only when free cash flow after capex covers the dividend comfortably, so the yield signal is a claim on sustainable cash rather than a trap.
groups.why: Mature payers with discipline; weak valuation.

examples: Dividend payers whose earnings have never turned negative over five years are the most sustainable distributors, and the market underreacts to their durability.
Firms whose dividend yield has never dropped below a high floor over five years, measured relative to industry peers, behave as stable income assets with lower crash risk.
groups.why: Stable payouts signal quality; no valuation.

examples: Stable payers that rarely pay out more in dividends than they earn are a durable low-risk group, while firms that repeatedly paid dividends above earnings are funding distributions from balance sheets and face a higher c
groups.why: Avoids dividends exceeding earnings; stable payers.

examples: Yield earned by firms that have paid common dividends for many of the last five years reflects a credible, institutionalized payout policy that managers are reluctant to break.
Firms that combine a high current yield with a multi-year record of raising dividends are mature cash generators whose boards are signaling rising confidence in future earnings.
groups.why: Yield and payout record; owner alignment.

examples: A high dividend yield only signals value when the balance sheet is not stretched, so the yield is counted only for firms with long-term debt below 25% of assets.
Firms that have paid dividends in most of the last five years and whose peak long-term leverage over that window stayed low signal durable financial discipline, which the market underprices.
groups.why: Yield with low leverage; discount plus discipline.

examples: Firms that have paid dividends in most of the last five years and whose weakest operating cash flow yield over that window was still high have the most credible, habit-driven payout policy.
Dividends are a more reliable quality signal when the profit stream behind them is stable, so the highest subsequent returns come from high-payout firms whose ROA volatility over five years is low.
groups.why: Dividends backed by persistent profit; quality.

groups.area: Dividends covered by steady cash flow
examples: Firms whose worst five-year dividend coverage remains high have dividends that survived past downturns, which signals a durable payout policy that the market underprices.
When operating cash flow is growing faster than dividends, the payout is becoming safer over time, and this improving-coverage trajectory predicts positive abnormal returns.
groups.why: Covered dividends signal quality and alignment.

groups.area: Dividends covered by steady cash flow
examples: When dividends grow faster than operating cash flow, payouts are being pushed ahead of the cash that funds them, which leads to later dividend reversals, equity issuance or leverage, and underperformance over the followi
groups.why: Avoids dividends outrunning cash; prudent allocation.

examples: The size of the dividend shortfall relative to the size of the accrual gap measures how much of reported earnings is non-cash yet distributed to shareholders.
When leverage is high, a dividend financed beyond operating cash flow competes directly with debt service and covenant headroom, making the payout more likely to be cut.
groups.why: Avoids non-cash earnings paid out; quality and prudence.

groups.area: Durable gross margins in knowledge firms
examples: Firms whose gross margin is both high and steady within their industry hold pricing power, and the market underprices how durable that margin is over a 12-month horizon.
Within an industry, firms that sustain high five-year R&D intensity while keeping their gross margin stable convert knowledge spending into durable pricing power, which the market prices slowly.
groups.why: Durable pricing power supports business quality.

examples: Earnings increases are underpriced most in cheap stocks, where investors anchor on depressed prices and under-update to a better earnings trajectory.
A persistent, multi-year rise in operating cash-generating power per dollar of equity value signals a durable repricing that markets absorb gradually.
groups.why: Earnings gains in cheap stocks; discount element.

examples: The mismatch is sharper in changes than in levels. When year-over-year cash-flow shocks are much more volatile than earnings shocks, earnings are being cushioned by accruals, and that cushioning is expected to unwind.

Smoothing is most informative for levered firms. Debt covenants and refinancing needs give managers the strongest incentive to flatten reported earnings, so the earnings-to-cash volatility gap is most diagnostic where lo
groups.why: Buys smoothed earnings suggesting manipulation; management quality.

examples: Firms whose operating cash flow is much more volatile than their reported earnings are smoothing income, and their future earnings tend to disappoint.
Smoothing matters most when it coincides with a multi-year build-up of positive accruals, meaning reported earnings persistently run ahead of cash generation.
groups.why: Avoids income smoothers; management quality.

examples: The best value opportunities combine a high earnings yield with improving return on assets, because the market has not yet priced a fundamental turnaround.
Earnings yield is only a reliable value signal when the earnings are backed by positive operating cash flow; cheap stocks with negative operating cash flow are value traps.
groups.why: Earnings yield value; discount to intrinsic value.

examples: When the depreciation rate falls, the firm is effectively lengthening asset lives, which lowers expense and lifts earnings without any change in operations.
Firms whose receivables grow faster than sales are more likely to be recognizing revenue early or loosely, and the market underreacts to this signal in the year it appears.
groups.why: Avoids manipulation; management quality.

examples: Firms that have reported an effective tax rate above 25% in many of the last five years are not relying on recurring tax shelters, so their earnings are of higher quality and their future returns are higher.

Among firms with positive pre-tax income, a high effective tax rate relative to industry peers signals that the firm is not sheltering profits, so its earnings are more likely to be cash-backed and sustained.
groups.why: High tax signals earnings quality; no valuation.

examples: Cheap enterprise value matters most when the EBITDA is converted into operating cash, because accrual-heavy EBITDA tends to reverse and does not reflect real value.
A cheap EBITDA yield is only a real bargain when reported EBITDA turns into operating cash flow; otherwise the cheapness reflects accrual-driven earnings that revert.
groups.why: Cheap EV with cash conversion; discount plus quality.

groups.area: Enterprise sales yield backed by cash
examples: Within each industry, firms with high enterprise sales yield and a cash-to-current-liabilities floor that has held up over five years should outperform.
The sum of within-industry z-scores for sales yield and cash cover identifies firms that are cheap on revenue and also hold liquid balance sheets relative to their sector peers.
groups.why: Cheap on sales with liquid balance sheet.

examples: Stocks whose earnings yield exceeds the firm's implied cost of debt are underpriced relative to credit, so equity should earn higher subsequent returns.
Equity that has stayed cheap relative to credit for three consecutive years, not just in one year, signals durable mispricing that the market corrects slowly.
groups.why: Equity cheap versus credit; discount to value.

examples: An issuance spike is informative when it is abnormal relative to the firm's own recent issuance intensity, not when a habitual issuer raises capital at a steady pace.
Firms that issue net equity after a strong prior-year run-up are exploiting a window of high valuation, and the subsequent return reversal should be concentrated in these firms.
groups.why: Avoids opportunistic issuers; shareholder alignment.

examples: Stocks with strong prior twelve-month returns that have not issued equity are less likely to be overvalued and more likely to continue rising through information diffusion. Equity issuance after a rally is the managerial
groups.why: Non-issuers align with owners; prior winners not value.

examples: Persistent equity raising over three years that exceeds cumulative R&D spending signals opportunistic capital raising, and the market under-reacts to this multi-year pattern.
Persistent multi-year equity raising that is not matched by sustained R&D reflects a repeated market-timing pattern, not a one-off financing need, and predicts low subsequent returns.
groups.why: Avoids opportunistic equity raisers; alignment.

examples: Firms that issue equity while already trading at high market-to-book are selling shares into overvaluation, and the stock tends to underperform as the mispricing corrects.
Sustained multi-year equity raising, rather than a one-off issue, signals a persistent reliance on external equity at market prices, which predicts weak subsequent returns.
groups.why: Avoids issuing into overvaluation; alignment and discount.

groups.area: Expensive firms in a capex surge
examples: Relative to peers in the same industry, firms that are simultaneously more expensive on sales and making a larger capex jump than their own history are overvalued expansion stories.
Expensive firms whose capex grows faster than sales are building capacity ahead of demand, and the market's optimism about the investment fails to be validated by revenue, leading to lower returns.
groups.why: Avoids expensive overbuilders; discount and discipline.

examples: Expensive firms that burn operating cash and must raise equity to fund it are overpriced relative to their fundamentals, and the market corrects this over time.
Firms that come to market after a strong price run-up are exploiting a window of high investor sentiment, and the resulting capital raises mark prices that will revert.
groups.why: Avoids expensive raisers; discount and alignment.

groups.area: Expensive firms with persistent debt issuance
examples: Within an industry, firms that are richly valued relative to peers and that borrow more persistently than peers are funding valuation rather than cash flow, and their subsequent returns are weaker.
The valuation premium matters for returns only when a firm has been a net debt raiser over the past three years, because debt-funded expansion signals that the premium is financed rather than earned.
groups.why: Avoids expensive debt-funded firms; discount and prudence.

examples: A firm lagging its industry in both cash ROA and accounting ROA is under-reacting to an industry-wide improvement, and the lag is more likely to close when both channels confirm it.
Over a two-year window, smoothed ROA that lags the industry's improvement predicts catch-up, but only for firms that are not deeply loss-making, since distressed firms may keep deteriorating.
groups.why: Laggards may be undervalued; weak on quality.

examples: Firms that repurchase stock in many of the last five years while their earnings swing widely have built a habit of flexible payout that the market discounts as temporary.
Volatility in operating cash flow, rather than accounting earnings, is the relevant trigger for valuing buyback-based flexibility, because cash shortfalls are what force payout cuts.
groups.why: Repurchasing habit shows alignment; volatile earnings weaken quality.

examples: Firms with high free cash flow yield and a low level of intangible assets relative to total assets are mispriced because investors pay for tangible earnings power less than they should.
Cheap free cash flow is only a reliable signal of mispricing when the firm is not spending on acquisitions; cash flow that is later recycled into M&A is not fully available to shareholders.
groups.why: Cheap FCF without M&A; discount and discipline.

examples: Cash-flow volatility matters most for firms carrying heavy long-term debt, because unstable operating cash can threaten debt service and force distress-like discounting.
Volatile cash flows matter most for firms that are richly valued relative to book equity, since their prices embed growth expectations that unstable cash generation can fail to support.
groups.why: Avoids volatile cash flows; business quality.

examples: The preferred-claim burden is more dangerous when it is large both against total assets and against the common equity base, because the two scales capture different parts of the dilution problem.
Within each industry, firms whose preferred stock and minority interests take a larger share of book assets leave less residual value for common shareholders, so they underperform over the next year.
groups.why: Avoids claims diluting common shareholders; alignment.

examples: Expensive firms whose accrual ratio is highly volatile over five years have unreliable, managed earnings, and the market's high multiple does not price in the instability of the earnings stream.
Glamour stocks whose accruals have been positive for several years are the most overpriced, since persistent accrual buildup signals aggressive accounting that markets fail to discount over time.
groups.why: Avoids expensive aggressive accounting; discount and quality.

examples: Acquisition intensity matters mainly when the acquirer's stock is expensive, because high-multiple firms can use overvalued shares as currency to buy assets at inflated prices.

Firms that add intangible capital (largely acquired goodwill and intangibles) while already trading at high market-to-book within their industry overpay for growth, so their subsequent returns are low.
groups.why: Avoids overpaying acquirers; capital allocation and discount.

examples: Intangible-heavy firms whose near-term debt is large relative to their cash face a refinancing squeeze, and a forced sale or equity issue at depressed prices hurts subsequent returns.
Intangible-heavy firms with more short-term debt than cash face a refinancing wall. If credit tightens, they must sell assets or issue equity at depressed prices, which weighs on subsequent returns.
groups.why: Avoids fragile goodwill-heavy firms; quality.

groups.area: Gross margin growth over sales growth
examples: Firms whose gross margin has expanded in many of the last five fiscal years show a durable competitive advantage that the market underreacts to, so they outperform.
Gross profit dollars growing faster than net sales dollars, scaled by total assets, signals operating leverage and pricing power that precede positive abnormal returns.
groups.why: Pricing power signals business quality.

groups.area: Gross profit per dollar of total investment
examples: A firm whose gross-profit-to-investment ratio is at a high point relative to its own five-year history signals improving reinvestment efficiency that the market has not yet fully priced.
The payoff to gross profit per investment dollar is strongest when it is accompanied by stable gross profitability on assets, since volatile margins indicate that the high ratio may be transitory.
groups.why: Capital efficiency signals quality.

examples: Profitable firms that repurchase shares in many of the last five years are signaling a durable, committed payout policy backed by stable gross profits, which the market underprices.
Firms with high gross profitability that also repurchase heavily over the past three years are undervalued and confident in their cash generation, so their future returns should be high.
groups.why: Profitable buyers; quality and alignment.

examples: Firms whose gross profitability has never dropped below a floor over five years and that repaid debt in many of those years have durable, self-funding operations, which the market underprices.

Firms with high gross profitability that are increasing their debt repayment rate are moving toward a lower-risk financial position, and investors who anchor on past leverage under-react to this change in direction.
groups.why: Profitable deleveraging; quality.

groups.area: Gross profit with low total leverage
examples: Gross profitability that is stable over five years, combined with low debt, signals a durable franchise whose cash flows are priced as if they were riskier than they are.
Gross profitability predicts returns only among firms whose debt load is modest, because for heavily levered firms gross profits are absorbed by interest and refinancing risk.
groups.why: Profitable low-debt franchises; quality.

examples: High gross profitability matters most when the firm keeps a high gross margin, because that signals pricing power rather than high throughput on thin margins.
Firms whose gross profitability has never dipped below a high level over the past three years have durable competitive advantages that the market under-prices.
groups.why: Gross profitability durable; quality.

examples: Firms whose gross profitability is trending up over five years and that spend heavily on R&D relative to sales are converting innovation into expanding margins, and this trajectory is underpriced.

Firms that have spent on R&D persistently over five years, and that keep investing in fixed capital, are building future productive capacity that the market under-reacts to, so they earn higher returns.
groups.why: Quality growth; not value-oriented.

groups.area: Harvesting: capex below depreciation at high margins
examples: Firms that have spent less than depreciation for many of the last five years while maintaining operating margins have settled into a harvest regime, a durable state that the market treats as ex-growth and therefore under

Harvesting is a standing policy, not a one-year event. Firms that have spent below depreciation in most of the last five years, and that also earn high operating margins, have a committed cash-return posture that the mar
groups.why: Harvesting profitable firms; cash returned to owners.

groups.area: Harvesting: capex below depreciation at high margins
examples: Firms that spend above depreciation in most of the last five years while sustaining high gross margins are committing to a long-run expansion path that the market reprices slowly, producing lower future returns.

Capex-to-depreciation only signals harvesting when operating margins are high. Low-margin firms with low capex are shrinking or distressed, and that is a different mechanism that should not be mixed into the long side.
groups.why: Buys expansion at high margins; tenets ambiguous.

examples: Within an industry, firms that build intangibles faster than peers while converting less of their assets into operating cash are the most overvalued relative to their own sector's cash economics.

Firms that add intangible assets while generating little operating cash flow are likely overpaying for acquired or capitalized intangibles, and the value shortfall shows up as lower subsequent returns.
groups.why: Avoids overpaid intangibles; capital allocation discipline.

examples: Firms that have paid a high implied rate on debt for several consecutive years carry structural, not transitory, credit risk that the market discounts slowly.
A rising implied cost of debt signals that lenders are repricing a firm's credit risk upward, and equity investors adjust slowly, so stocks with widening borrowing costs underperform.
groups.why: Avoids high credit risk; business quality.

groups.area: Improving interest cover with debt reduction
examples: A sustained multi-year rise in interest cover matters most when the firm is actually retiring debt, so the trend signal is conditional on net repayment.
Stocks where operating income is growing while interest expense is shrinking show a divergence that signals improving financial health and future earnings power.
groups.why: Improving coverage with deleveraging; quality.

examples: Within each industry, firms whose operating margin on assets has been rising for five years and whose net working capital is improving are building momentum in fundamentals that the market prices slowly.

Profitable firms that are reducing their total liability burden relative to assets are improving both profitability and solvency simultaneously, and the market prices this combined improvement with a lag.
groups.why: Improving profit and solvency; quality.

examples: Firms whose net fixed plant is growing fastest within their industry are adding physical productive capacity, and this capacity is sunk and later pressures industry prices and returns.
A firm that is both growing its asset base fast and spending heavily on capex relative to its industry is in the middle of a build-out boom, and such build-outs are overpriced at the peak.
groups.why: Avoids overbuilding; capital allocation discipline.

examples: A firm whose split-adjusted share count grows faster than its industry median is issuing into a sector-wide hot market, so its shares are relatively overpriced and subsequent returns are low.
When a firm's share issuance is accelerating faster than its industry median, it is front-running the peak of a sector issuance wave, and the subsequent price correction produces low returns.
groups.why: Avoids issuers into hot markets; alignment.

examples: Within industries that have fallen, firms that still generate positive operating cash flow are mispriced and recover more strongly.
When an industry is sold off, firms that cut capital spending relative to their peers signal capacity exit, and the industry recovers as supply shrinks.
groups.why: Buys industries with stronger prior returns; patience-for-discount tenet disfavors.

examples: Industry momentum is more persistent when fundamental sales growth within the industry confirms the price move, reflecting real sector news rather than sentiment.
Industry momentum diffuses more slowly into the prices of levered firms, so the momentum effect should be concentrated among low-leverage firms within each industry.
groups.why: Momentum chasing contradicts discount-to-value approach.

examples: Sector-wide demand trends show up in the industry median of smoothed sales growth, and this median predicts next-month returns for firms in that sector.
Industry-ranked sales growth predicts returns only when the firm's own sales are actually expanding, so the signal should be gated by positive own-firm growth.
groups.why: Industry sales momentum not addressed.

examples: When an industry rises, firms that have not yet moved as much as their peers underreact to the common news and catch up over the following year.
An industry shock that is large relative to a stock's normal volatility is a clearer signal of sector-wide fundamental news, and that news continues.
groups.why: Buys recent industry winners; contradicts discount buying.

groups.area: Industry-relative cash yield minus Sloan accruals
examples: Stocks with a high three-year cumulative operating cash flow yield and a low one-year change in working capital, both ranked within industry, are undervalued relative to peers.
Industry-relative cash yield only predicts returns when the firm's three-year average accrual ratio is negative, meaning cash earnings have consistently exceeded reported earnings.
groups.why: Cash yield cheap with clean accruals; discount plus quality.

examples: Empire builders are firms that grow their asset base faster than peers while earning below-peer returns on those assets, so a high score on industry-relative profitability combined with low industry-relative growth ident
groups.why: Avoids empire builders; capital discipline.

examples: Firms growing their asset base much faster than industry peers are empire building, and their subsequent returns are lower than those of peers with similar growth in the broader market.
A firm that is sharply stepping up its capital spending relative to its own past, and more than its peers are, is experiencing a late-cycle investment surge that tends to precede low returns.
groups.why: Avoids empire building; capital allocation.

examples: A firm that is stepping up its equity issuance faster than its industry peers is accelerating into a valuation peak, and its future returns are weaker.
Firms that dilute faster than peers while trading at a high market-to-book relative to their industry are exploiting temporarily high prices, so their future returns are low.
groups.why: Avoids diluters at high valuations; alignment.

examples: Firms whose worst operating margin in the last three years still beats their industry peers have a structural cost position that survives downturns.
Firms whose gross margin is rising faster than their industry peers are gaining pricing power or cost advantages that the market prices in gradually.
groups.why: Margin advantage supports business quality.

examples: Firms whose gross margins are unusually stable compared with industry peers have more predictable cash flows and lower risk premia, so they earn lower subsequent returns when margin volatility is high relative to peers.
groups.why: Low premium for stable margins; tenets silent.

examples: Within-industry cheapness predicts returns only among firms with positive profitability on book equity; cheap firms with losses are value traps that continue to underperform.
Industry-cheap stocks whose operating cash flow per asset is rising are value opportunities, while cheap stocks with deteriorating cash generation are value traps that remain cheap.
groups.why: Industry-cheap with improving cash; discount plus quality.

examples: An R&D-led marketing mix pays off only when the product carries high gross margins, so the innovation tilt should be rewarded mainly among firms with pricing power.
Firms that have been steadily shifting their spending mix from selling toward R&D over five years are reallocating toward intangible capital, and the market underprices that multi-year transition.
groups.why: Spending mix not addressed.

examples: Firms whose R&D intensity is stable over five years are running committed, long-horizon innovation programs, whereas firms with erratic R&D are cutting and restoring spending to manage earnings, so the stable firms shoul

When SG&A intensity is decelerating, meaning the firm is ceasing to add selling cost faster than revenue, marketing spend is being pared back and the freed resources flow to productive use, while firms whose selling inte
groups.why: R&D stability and SG&A trend not addressed.

examples: When an intangible-heavy firm's tax bill is rising relative to assets, its reported earnings are catching up to a growing underlying cash-generating franchise that the market has not yet priced.

Firms with a large, smoothed intangible asset base that have paid taxes in every one of the last five years hold durable, taxable intangible franchises, which the market discounts as accounting noise.
groups.why: Taxpaying intangible franchises; quality.

examples: Intangibility matters for returns only when the firm's cash generation exceeds reported income, so the intangible tilt is gated on a positive cash surplus over earnings.
Cash-backed earnings that recur across years signal durable economic value in intangible-heavy firms, whereas a single year of cash backing can be transitory working-capital timing.
groups.why: Cash-backed earnings; quality.

examples: Scaling the accrual gap by the intangible base rather than by total assets shows how much reported earnings exceed cash per dollar of intangible capital; firms with the lowest accrual-per-intangible-dollar should outperf
groups.why: Low accrual per intangible; earnings quality.

examples: Firms that have reported R&D in most of the last five years, and that trade at high book-to-market, have durable knowledge assets the market prices as if they were obsolete.
The earnings yield predicts returns only among firms whose assets are predominantly intangible, where book-based value measures are most distorted and price errors are largest.
groups.why: High book-to-market knowledge assets; discount.

examples: Among levered firms, where debt is above 30% of assets, the cross-section of interest coverage matters most for equity value, so high-coverage levered firms earn a risk-adjusted premium.
Stocks that cover interest both with accounting operating profit and with actual operating cash flow are safer, and the agreement between the two measures is a stronger signal than either alone.
groups.why: Interest coverage supports quality; no valuation.

examples: When interest expense is growing faster than operating profit, a firm's debt service is becoming more burdensome and fragility is rising. Firms with the largest gap between interest growth and profit growth should underp
groups.why: Avoids rising debt burden; quality.

examples: Intermediate momentum per unit of trailing volatility is a cleaner predictor than raw 6-1 return, because high-volatility winners are partly compensated risk or lottery-like noise.
Intermediate momentum is more persistent in low-leverage firms because their equity is not subject to distress-driven forced selling or refinancing shocks that interrupt price trends.
groups.why: Momentum chasing contradicts discount purchase.

examples: R&D intensity is rewarded most when operating cash flow covers the R&D budget, since then the research engine is paid for by the business itself rather than by outside capital.
Firms that spend heavily on R&D relative to sales without issuing equity fund their innovation from internal resources, and the market under-prices this self-financed research engine.
groups.why: Self-funded R&D; capital discipline.

examples: A rising inventory-to-sales ratio relative to industry peers indicates a firm-specific stock build that precedes markdowns and lower returns.
Among firms with positive operating profitability, inventory growing faster than sales signals demand softening that will compress margins and depress future returns.
groups.why: Avoids inventory build; business quality.

examples: Within its industry, a firm whose inventory-to-sales ratio is rising while it carries heavy R&D capital is likely building stock that customers have not absorbed.
Inventory outgrowing sales matters for returns mainly when the firm is R&D-heavy, because there the inventory is the output of a development program that is failing to sell.
groups.why: Avoids inventory build in R&D firms; quality.

groups.area: Inventory piling up against cost of goods
examples: Inventory building faster than COGS is most dangerous when top-line sales are shrinking, because the goods are not moving and management is likely to face write-downs.
A rising multi-year trend in inventory relative to COGS, expressed as implied days on hand, signals that a firm is losing control of working capital and will face demand-driven markdowns.
groups.why: Avoids inventory buildup; quality.

examples: Firms that have generated positive free cash flow in every one of the last three years are funding their investment internally and can return capital without relying on capital markets. Using the three-year minimum rathe

Firms that generate operating cash flow in excess of capital spending and avoid raising external capital are self-financing their growth, and the market underprices that discipline. The strategy owns the fifth with the h
groups.why: Self-financing firms; owner-like discipline.

examples: Firms whose capital spending exceeds operating cash flow and that simultaneously raise external capital are overinvesting with borrowed or issued money, which predicts underperformance.
Investment intensity matters for returns only when the firm is a net external financier in the current year; net issuers that also expand capital spending are the ones that underperform.
groups.why: Avoids overinvestment funded externally.

examples: Within an industry, firms that spend heavily on capital expenditure while generating weak operating cash flow relative to assets destroy value, so their subsequent returns are low.
Stocks in the top tail of both capital intensity and weak operating cash generation are empire-building firms whose investment is not backed by cash earnings, so they underperform.
groups.why: Avoids empire building without cash backing.

groups.area: Investment out of step with peers
examples: Firms that are adding capacity fast relative to their existing fixed-asset base and their industry peers are over-expanding, which predicts low future returns.
Firms whose three-year average of total investment, including acquisitions, runs well above their industry's norm are over-expanding and destroy value relative to peers.
groups.why: Avoids over-expansion; capital discipline.

examples: Investment is value-destroying mainly when it is not funded by internal cash generation, so high net investment combined with negative operating cash flow predicts the lowest returns.
Persistent investment over three years, rather than a single-year spike, identifies firms with a durable empire-building or capacity-expansion stance that the market fails to fully price.
groups.why: Avoids overinvestment; capital discipline.

examples: Equity issuance by firms whose market value is far above book value is an overvaluation signal, and these firms earn low subsequent returns.
Firms that have diluted repeatedly over three years and also sit near a 12-month price peak are habitual market-timers whose returns are persistently low.
groups.why: Avoids issuers after run-ups; alignment.

examples: Within each industry, firms that issue equity while also carrying the highest market-to-book relative to peers are the most overvalued and underperform.
Within each industry, firms that both issue equity and trade at elevated book multiples are the most overvalued relative to peers and should underperform.
groups.why: Avoids expensive issuers; discount and alignment.

examples: Firms that issue equity and also build cash within their industry are raising capital without a deployment plan, and their subsequent returns are lower.
Five-year cumulative equity issuance matters most when it coincides with an actual year-over-year cash increase, which signals that proceeds were kept rather than spent.
groups.why: Avoids raising capital without use; alignment.

groups.area: Knowledge stock with cash cover of liabilities
examples: R&D-intensive firms whose cash-plus-R&D cover of liabilities is stable across years are less likely to be distressed in substance, so their accounting leverage is misread by investors who price it as fragility.

Firms that combine a heavy, cumulative knowledge investment with a high floor on knowledge-adjusted cover are accounting-distressed and should outperform, and the two channels confirm each other when they coincide.
groups.why: Financial strength in R&D firms; quality.

groups.area: Knowledge stock with cash cover of liabilities
examples: R&D-heavy firms whose knowledge-adjusted cover is volatile over five years carry hidden fragility that the market penalizes, so the signal selects the low-volatility end of this distribution, which is the more reliably s
groups.why: Low volatility cover; quality.

groups.area: Knowledge stock with gross-profit cover of liabilities
examples: Firms with a large cumulative R&D stock whose gross-profit-to-liability cover has been trending upward over five years are building a knowledge base that is increasingly self-financed, which the market underprices.

A firm that is spending on R&D at a high point relative to its own five-year history, and that has high current gross-profit cover of liabilities, is building its knowledge base from a position of financial strength.
groups.why: Self-financed knowledge base; quality.

examples: Firms whose knowledge-inclusive operating margin is accelerating while capex growth is slowing are experiencing improving returns on invested capital, which the market prices with a delay.
Disciplined compounders combine high R&D-adjusted operating return on assets with low capex relative to depreciation, and both traits are more informative when judged against industry peers.
groups.why: Disciplined compounders; quality.

examples: Firms whose R&D intensity is accelerating while capex-to-assets is falling are entering a phase of investment reorientation that the market prices only after it shows up in margins.
A firm that has accumulated more five-year R&D relative to five-year capex is building a scalable intangible asset base that the market prices below its eventual cash-flow contribution.
groups.why: R&D versus capex mix not addressed.

examples: A sudden jump in acquisition intensity marks a new strategic deal wave that the market underreacts to, so returns are lower in the months after the shift.
Large acquisitions paid for with newly issued equity signal that management views its own shares as overvalued, and the market subsequently corrects this.
groups.why: Avoids acquisition waves; management discipline.

examples: Firms with persistently high and erratic leverage, meaning large swings in liabilities-to-assets across years, carry refinancing and covenant risk that the market fails to price in advance.
Leverage is most dangerous for firms that are already losing money, because equity holders absorb losses on a shrinking base and the market tends to under-react to this combined deterioration.
groups.why: Avoids high erratic leverage; quality.

groups.area: Leverage adjusted for the hidden knowledge stock
examples: Firms whose knowledge-adjusted leverage is rising, through debt growth outpacing the growth of intangible capital, are moving into fragility and should underperform.
Adjusted leverage predicts negative returns mainly when a firm is currently loss-making, because distress converts a knowledge-inflated balance sheet into a real refinancing and default risk.
groups.why: Avoids fragile leverage; quality.

examples: Net debt scaled by market equity captures the market-based leverage that equity holders bear, and its excess over industry peers predicts lower returns.
Leverage above industry peers combined with operating profitability below industry peers marks a distress state where debt service is fragile and returns are depressed.
groups.why: Avoids excess leverage; quality.

examples: A stock that has both a deep stock of retained earnings and a steadily improving net return on assets carries two independent signs of durable profitability that the market prices only gradually.

The retained-earnings record predicts returns only when operating profitability is currently improving; among firms with a long earnings history but flat or falling operating margins, the signal should be neutral.
groups.why: Durable profitability; quality.

examples: Stocks that combine rapid five-year sales growth with a high current market value relative to sales are priced for continued extrapolation, so their growth premium is later reversed.
Firms that have grown sales in most of the last five years, and whose five-year growth is high, are the classic glamour names whose persistence is over-trusted, so they underperform.
groups.why: Avoids expensive glamour growth; discount tenet.

examples: Stocks with poor five-year returns whose return on assets has just improved are early-stage recoveries that the market under-reacts to.
The long-run reversal effect is concentrated among high-volatility losers, where investor over-reaction and limits to arbitrage are largest.
groups.why: Buys long-term losers; contrarian discount.

examples: Firms that have climbed off their recent three-year profitability trough, after a long price decline, are mispriced because investors keep anchoring on the trough.
Stocks that have underperformed for years but whose sales per dollar of assets are rising are recovering operationally, and their prices lag the operating improvement.
groups.why: Beaten-down with improving fundamentals; discount and quality.

examples: Stocks priced below ten dollars with high recent volatility attract retail gambling flows and become overpriced relative to their expected payoff.
Low-priced stocks with negative earnings are the purest lottery tickets, because their payoff depends on a future turnaround that investors overprice.
groups.why: Buys lottery stocks and speculative turnarounds; quality criteria.

examples: A sub-$5 stock whose price has recently jumped is an attention-driven lottery ticket. Gamblers chase these rallies, pushing prices above fundamental value, and the premium reverses over the next year.

Low-priced firms with weak earnings are the most likely lottery candidates. Investors buy them for a small chance of a turnaround, so their prices embed a premium that fades as the turnaround fails to arrive.
groups.why: Avoids speculative lottery stocks; quality.

examples: High volatility combined with high leverage signals distress-like lottery payoffs, and investors overpay for these equity claims, so they underperform.
Expensive stocks with high volatility, meaning low book-to-market, are where investors pay the most for lottery-like upside, producing the weakest subsequent returns.
groups.why: Avoids expensive volatile lottery stocks; discount.

examples: Stocks that are cheap on operating earnings yield and whose return on tangible capital is rising are early in an earnings recovery that the market has not fully priced.
Cheap operating earnings count as a genuine bargain only when the business earns a high return on its tangible capital base; cheap earnings from low-return businesses are value traps.
groups.why: Cheap with high returns on capital; discount plus quality.

examples: A sustained, multi-year rise in asset turnover combined with a stable operating margin signals durable operating efficiency that the market prices only gradually.
Asset turnover gains accompanied by a falling operating margin signal volume-driven growth on a depressed margin base, which should precede margin recovery and higher returns.
groups.why: Operating efficiency supports quality.

examples: Within an industry, firms whose gross debt is small relative to market value have more equity cushion and lower distress risk, and the market under-reacts to this gap over the next year.
Firms whose market leverage has been trending upward over five years, typically because equity value erodes while debt is maintained, experience a persistent distress drift and underperform.
groups.why: Avoids high market leverage; quality.

groups.area: Market leverage with net debt repayment
examples: High market leverage combined with a recent decline in book leverage marks firms where the market has not yet rewarded a visible reduction in the liability burden.
Persistent multi-year debt paydown among industry-relative high market-leverage firms signals a sustained balance-sheet repair that the market only gradually recognizes.
groups.why: Leveraged firms repairing balance sheet; cheap.

examples: Twelve-month price winners that also earn a gross margin above 30% of assets keep outperforming, while winners without that base of profitability fade.
Twelve-month momentum is rewarded only when the firm clears a minimum gross-profitability hurdle; among firms below the hurdle, past winners do not continue to outperform.
groups.why: Momentum buying contradicts discount to intrinsic value.

examples: Net cash is a safety margin only when the business is earning a profit; cash-rich firms that are loss-making tend to burn their cash and deserve no value credit.
Firms that have sustained a net cash position over several years, not just a single year-end, carry a durable balance-sheet cushion that the market under-credits.
groups.why: Net cash cushion relative to price; discount and quality.

examples: Rapid accumulation of net cash signals empire-building or agency-driven hoarding of cash, which the market penalizes, so firms whose net cash is falling (paying down debt or distributing cash) outperform firms that are r
groups.why: Avoiding cash accumulators; tenets ambiguous.

groups.area: Net cash yield with low working-capital accruals
examples: Net cash yield is more reliable when working-capital restraint has persisted for several years, not just in one year.
Stocks with high net cash relative to market value outperform, but only when their non-cash working capital is being released or held flat rather than built up.
groups.why: Net cash cheapness with accrual discipline.

examples: Asset-backed value stocks that have not collapsed over the past year are stabilizing, and the market has not yet confirmed a distress narrative that would trap the value.
A firm whose net current asset cushion is both large relative to price and steadily rebuilding over five years is recovering balance-sheet strength that analysts have not yet credited.
groups.why: Net current asset value; deep discount.

examples: Firms that issue net external capital while their stock has run up are selling overpriced shares to investors, so the subsequent return is weakest for this combination.
Net external financing scaled by the current monthly market equity measures how much new capital the firm has raised relative to its present valuation, and high values predict low returns.
groups.why: Avoids external financing; alignment.

examples: Operating assets that remain high while sales contract represent idle capital whose returns are deteriorating, and the market is slow to mark down the value of such assets.
Bloat that persists is more damaging than a single year of expansion, so firms with high NOA levels that have grown NOA in each of the last three years underperform most strongly.
groups.why: Avoids bloated operating assets; discipline.

groups.area: Net operating assets plus net external financing
examples: Firms whose net operating assets are high relative to their industry peers, and that also raise net outside capital scaled by market value, are over-investing and will earn lower subsequent returns.

Firms whose net operating assets are growing quickly over time, rather than merely being large, are accumulating operating capital faster than their earnings justify, and subsequent returns are lower.
groups.why: Avoids overinvestors raising capital; discipline.

examples: Firms that issue equity in most of the last five years are serial issuers that keep diluting shareholders, and their returns are persistently poor.
Issuance matters most when it occurs at high market prices relative to book, because managers issue when shares are overvalued and the mispricing then reverses.
groups.why: Avoids dilution; shareholder alignment.

examples: Firms whose operating cash flow coverage of liabilities has been declining over five years, and which are small in size, face rising default risk that the market does not fully price.
Repeated losses over several years, combined with high liabilities relative to assets, signal a firm whose equity cushion is eroding, and the market reacts slowly to this persistent deterioration.
groups.why: Avoids bankruptcy-risk firms; quality.
