examples: Operating leverage matters most when demand is unstable, so firms combining heavy fixed costs with a history of volatile sales growth face the largest earnings risk and should earn a risk premium.

Operating leverage is most dangerous when high fixed costs sit on top of an unstable revenue base, so the premium is largest for firms that combine heavy fixed-cost intensity with volatile asset turnover.
groups.why: Buys fragile operating leverage with unstable sales; quality.

examples: Operating profitability backed by cash generation is more persistent than accounting profit alone, because accruals-driven profits tend to reverse.
Operating profit yield on market value, restricted to firms that are actually profitable, identifies stocks whose cash-earning power is cheap relative to price.
groups.why: Profit yield on price with cash backing; value and quality.

examples: Organization capital is most credible when a firm's SG&A intensity has been high and persistent over time, since one-off selling spikes do not build durable customer and brand capital.

Accumulated SG&A pays off mainly where gross margins are high enough to recover the cost of building brand and selling capacity, so organization capital should be rewarded only for firms with pricing power.
groups.why: Brand capital signals business quality.

groups.area: Overhead efficiency with a safe balance sheet
examples: Firms whose sales growth outpaces SG&A growth are gaining operating leverage, and this leverage is most durable when short-term debt is low.
Within-industry overhead efficiency only predicts returns when the firm carries little short-term debt; for levered firms, efficiency is not sufficient to earn a premium.
groups.why: Efficient overhead with safe balance sheet; quality.

groups.area: Overhead efficiency with a safe balance sheet
examples: Firms that spend less on SG&A per dollar of sales, relative to peers in their industry, and carry a smaller share of their current liabilities as short-term debt, are running leaner organizations with more flexible finan
groups.why: Lean-looking firms with low short-term debt; ambiguous direction.

examples: Payables stretch carries more negative information when the firm also holds little cash, because the supplier credit is then a substitute for liquidity rather than a discretionary timing choice.
Firms that add payables faster than their cost base, relative to industry peers, are stretching suppliers or relying on trade credit to cover cash shortfalls, which predicts lower future returns.
groups.why: Avoids stretching suppliers; quality.

examples: Firms paying out heavily while investing lightly are harvesting mature assets; the market may over-penalize the underinvestment and under-price the cash returned to shareholders.
Among profitable firms, those paying out a larger share of earnings within their industry signal managerial confidence in sustained cash generation, and the market underprices that signal.
groups.why: Payout signals owner orientation.

groups.area: Peer-relative profitability net of Sloan accruals
examples: Firms whose gross profitability is high versus peers and whose net income is largely matched by operating cash flow are the firms whose reported profits are most likely to persist.
Firms with high operating profit relative to assets, and whose reported earnings consist least of accruals as a share of earnings size, are the most reliable earners within their industry.
groups.why: Persistent cash-backed profits; quality.

examples: Among firms generating positive operating cash flow, those whose cash flow exceeds reported earnings by the largest proportion are the highest-quality earners and should outperform.
groups.why: Cash exceeding earnings; high earnings quality.

examples: A rising trend in the smoothed accrual share signals deteriorating earnings quality, and the market underreacts to this gradual deterioration.
Firms whose accrual share is volatile over time have unstable earnings quality, which investors discount because it raises uncertainty about the true earnings base.
groups.why: Avoids deteriorating accrual quality.

examples: Accruals matter for returns mainly when the firm is simultaneously absorbing outside money; in firms that are net repurchasers or deleveraging, the same accruals are not a sign of overpricing.

Accruals matter most for firms that keep returning to outside capital markets year after year, because repeated issuance while reporting non-cash earnings is the classic pattern of overvalued issuers.
groups.why: Avoids serial issuers with accruals; alignment.

examples: Liquidity only signals an underpriced cash cow when the firm has never had negative operating cash return over the past five years, so cash holdings are gated by a durability condition.
Liquidity predicts returns only for firms whose operating cash flow has stayed positive for three consecutive years; for cash-burning firms, cash on hand signals distress rather than a cushion.
groups.why: Persistent cash generators with liquidity; quality.

examples: Firms whose worst operating cash flow year is close to their average year have stable cash generation, and the market prices this stability too low.
Cash flow floors combined with stable, low accrual volatility identify earnings that are real and persistent, a combination the market under-prices.
groups.why: Stable real cash profits; quality.

examples: Simultaneous improvement in gross margin and asset turnover signals a genuine operating upturn, and the market under-reacts to it when reported earnings are backed by cash.
Book-to-market is a more reliable return predictor when the cheap stock is also financially sound, so the value premium is concentrated in value firms that pass basic quality tests.
groups.why: Cheap quality stocks; discount plus quality.

groups.area: Pre-financing cash profit with a working-capital buffer
examples: Firms whose pre-financing cash profit margin is stable over time and that hold a large working-capital cushion are more predictable operators, and investors underprice this predictability.
Cash profit is more valuable when the working-capital cushion is stable over time, because volatile liquidity signals hidden operating or financing strain that the market gradually recognizes.
groups.why: Predictable operators with cushion; quality.

examples: Momentum returns are earned mainly by low-leverage winners, because highly levered firms that rebound sharply are subject to distress-driven reversals and momentum crashes.
Price momentum persists mainly in firms whose past winning is backed by current earnings. Unprofitable past winners are more likely to be driven by speculative repricing that reverses.
groups.why: Momentum buying contradicts discount to value.

examples: Stocks ranking high on both twelve-month price momentum and asset-scaled revenue growth outperform those strong on only one of the two.
Momentum is more persistent when earnings are backed by operating cash flow, meaning the stock's gain is supported by low accruals relative to its industry peers.
groups.why: Momentum focus contradicts discount approach.

examples: Near-high prices combined with a rising five-year trend in operating cash-generating margin signal that the market is slow to recognize a durable improvement in operating economics.
Firms whose split-adjusted price sits near its five-year maximum are under-reacting to news because investors anchor on the prior peak, so they continue to drift upward relative to peers.
groups.why: Buys stocks near highs; opposes discount buying.

examples: The worst gross margin a firm has posted in the last five years reveals its pricing floor. A firm whose trough margin stays high retains pricing power even in downturns.
Stable gross margins matter most when they sit on a large gross profit base, so the stability signal should be read only for firms earning at least 0.3 of assets as gross profit.
groups.why: Pricing power floor signals quality.

examples: When gross margin varies little even though sales growth is volatile, the firm is absorbing demand swings without pushing discounts through to margin, which signals pricing power that the market mistakes for cyclicality.
groups.why: Low-premium stable margins; tenets silent.

groups.area: Profit after interest with low working-capital build
examples: Interest-burdened operating profitability predicts returns only in years when the firm is releasing working capital, because that is when earnings convert into free cash rather than into receivables and inventory.

Firms that combine high after-interest profitability with working capital well below its five-year peak are unwinding past investment in operating assets and are likely to convert earnings into cash over the next year.
groups.why: Cash-convertible profit; quality.

examples: Firms whose cumulative three-year operating profit is rising while their three-year external financing also accumulates are buying growth that is not sustained, and they underperform.
Operating profit growth that is accompanied by heavy equity and debt issuance reflects bought growth that the market overvalues, so the combined score predicts lower next-month returns.
groups.why: Avoids bought growth; alignment.

groups.area: Profit growth that comes from accruals
examples: The accrual-reversal penalty applies mainly when reported earnings are rising, so the cash-lag measure matters only in firms whose income is growing.
Within an industry, firms with unusually high accrual-based earnings relative to assets are overvalued because the accrual component of earnings reverses.
groups.why: Avoids accrual-driven earnings; quality.

examples: Profit improvement that shows up in most years, not just on average, signals a durable operating advantage that the market prices in gradually.
Profit improvement that comes without balance-sheet expansion reflects operating efficiency rather than capital-driven growth, and the market extrapolates it too little.
groups.why: Persistent profit improvement; quality.

examples: Levered firms with stable gross margins over five years are safer than leverage alone implies, and their stability is underpriced relative to the leverage penalty.
Gross profitability predicts returns only among firms whose liabilities exceed half of assets, where profits matter most for solvency and the market is slow to credit them.
groups.why: Profitable levered firms; quality but leverage.

examples: Firms whose return on assets is near the top of their own five-year range are at a temporary profitability peak, and that peak mean-reverts, so future returns are lower.
High profitability combined with unstable profitability history signals a fragile peak, so high-rank, high-volatility firms underperform as their earnings spikes revert.
groups.why: Avoids peak profitability; patience, quality.

examples: Gross profitability predicts returns more strongly among small firms, where investors attend less to profit information and arbitrage is slower.
Firms whose operating margin on assets has been improving steadily over five years are underpriced when small, because the trend is recognized gradually.
groups.why: Small-firm conditioning not addressed.

groups.area: Profitable and low net operating assets, both required
examples: Gross profitability predicts returns only among firms whose operating working capital is being released. Profitable firms that are building working capital have earnings that will be reversed by future accruals.

Firms whose operating profitability has never dropped below a threshold over the past three years, and that keep net operating assets lean, deliver persistent excess returns because their earnings base is durable.
groups.why: Durable profit with lean assets; quality.

groups.area: Profitable firms funding growth with new equity
examples: Within an industry, firms that issue equity persistently while earning high accounting returns are the ones whose managers are most likely to exploit a high share price, so they lag their peers.
Within an industry, firms that issue the most equity while also generating the most operating cash flow are exploiting a temporarily high valuation relative to peers, so their returns underperform.
groups.why: Avoids equity issuers timing highs; alignment.

examples: Firms that have sold equity over the past three years and are highly profitable are timing a high valuation, and their returns are lower going forward.
Firms that issue equity heavily while gross profit is expensive relative to market value are exploiting a temporarily rich valuation, so future returns are weak.
groups.why: Avoids equity timers; alignment.

examples: Within each industry, firms that generate more gross profit per dollar of enterprise value are underpriced relative to peers that deliver the same gross profit at a higher multiple.
High industry-relative gross profitability predicts returns only when margins are expanding, since rising margins signal that a profitable position is strengthening rather than eroding.
groups.why: Cheap gross profit relative to EV; value and quality.

examples: Firms that keep spending on R&D while their gross margin trends upward are converting intangibles into pricing power, and the market underreacts to that persistent improvement.
Within industries, profitable firms that have been increasing their R&D share of sales are shifting toward scalable intangibles, and the market prices the margin payoff with a lag.
groups.why: Profitable R&D investors; quality.

examples: Firms whose gross profitability has never dropped below a threshold over the past five years are less likely to be value traps, so their book-to-market premium is more reliable.
Profitable firms whose stock prices have lagged over the past year are mispriced, because investors have not yet updated for profitability that is already present in the financials.
groups.why: Profitable laggards, cheap; discount plus quality.

examples: Stable multi-year gross profitability combined with a multi-year record of low acquisition spending identifies firms whose advantage is persistent and not manufactured by purchases.
Firms whose gross profitability has been rising steadily over five years and whose largest five-year acquisition spend is small are building profits internally and should outperform.
groups.why: Internally built profits; capital discipline.

groups.area: Quality firms buy back, weak firms issue
examples: Buybacks only signal undervaluation when the firm can fund its total payout from operating cash; repurchases financed beyond operating cash flow are a stress signal and should not count.
A multi-year record of repurchasing and not issuing equity identifies managers who consistently run the firm for existing owners, and the market under-reacts to this persistent discipline.
groups.why: Cash-funded buybacks, no issuance; alignment.

examples: Companies whose cash return on assets fluctuates little over five years are higher quality and are underpriced relative to their steadiness.
Cheap gross profit relative to total enterprise claims predicts outperformance, but only among firms with enough current-asset liquidity to avoid being priced as distressed.
groups.why: Cheap quality; discount plus quality.

groups.area: R&D backed by a cash-flow floor
examples: The R&D stock is most credible as a source of future returns only when the cash-flow floor is also high relative to market value, so a firm must score well on both before the market's discount on R&D is unwarranted.

R&D intensity is rewarded only when the firm has never let operating cash flow fall below a meaningful positive floor over the past five years; otherwise the R&D is a speculative burn that the market rightly discounts.
groups.why: R&D with cash floor; quality.

examples: Within an industry, firms whose R&D intensity is rising while retained earnings relative to assets are eroding are mispriced relative to peers facing the same sector conditions.
When retained earnings erode, a firm whose R&D intensity has been trending upward is doubling down on research under pressure, which the market reads as a weak signal and so underreacts to.
groups.why: Buys R&D increases amid eroding retained earnings; quality concern.

groups.area: R&D firms that can cover their debt
examples: R&D intensity earns a premium only when operating cash flow comfortably covers total debt, because then the firm can keep funding research through a downturn without creditor-forced cuts.
Firms that report R&D in most years and whose debt coverage is stable over time run a consistent innovation program that is protected from financing shocks, and the market underprices this stability.
groups.why: R&D with debt coverage; quality.

examples: R&D intensity is rewarded only when the firm is free-cash-flow positive after capital expenditure; for cash-burning firms, high R&D signals financing risk rather than productive investment.
R&D intensity is rewarded only when operating cash flow covers current liabilities, because then research is financed without refinancing risk and the firm can keep investing through downturns.
groups.why: R&D with cash resilience; quality.

examples: Sharp year-over-year R&D increases predict higher returns only when the firm is R&D-intensive enough that the spending is a material strategic commitment rather than noise.
An acceleration in R&D spending relative to the asset base, meaning the pace of R&D growth is itself rising, identifies firms entering a new innovation phase whose returns lag the market.
groups.why: R&D increases not addressed.

examples: Stocks that combine high industry-relative R&D intensity with a rising five-year R&D trend are expanding their innovation base, which the market under-anticipates.
Firms that have reported positive R&D in most of the last five years and spend heavily on it are building a durable innovation pipeline that the market discounts as a one-off cost.
groups.why: R&D intensity not addressed.

groups.area: R&D only among firms with cash
examples: A sustained multi-year commitment to R&D, funded by a sustained cash buffer, signals a credible long-horizon program rather than a temporary spending spike.
R&D intensity is rewarded only when the firm holds enough liquid cash to carry projects to completion, so the R&D premium is concentrated in cash-rich innovators.
groups.why: R&D backed by cash; quality.

examples: R&D spending is productive only when the firm has never reported a loss in the past five years, so the R&D premium should appear only among persistently profitable innovators.
R&D that is reported persistently over several years signals a committed research program, and when earnings are smooth this program is more likely to be productive and under-priced.
groups.why: R&D at consistently profitable firms; quality.

examples: Within an industry, firms whose receivables grow faster than sales show weaker collection or revenue pulled forward, and subsequently earn lower returns.
A firm whose receivables-to-sales ratio sits near the top of its own five-year range relative to peers is accumulating uncollected revenue, which predicts underperformance.
groups.why: Avoids receivable inflation; quality.

examples: Firms that add the most to retained earnings each year relative to their market value are generating internally funded value that the price does not yet reflect.
Firms that are steadily adding to retained earnings relative to their market value, averaged over three years, are compounding retained profit faster than their price reflects.
groups.why: Retained earnings relative to price; value and quality.

groups.area: Return driven by assets, not leverage
examples: A rising five-year trend in asset returns is more informative when the firm is lightly levered, because improvement in that case reflects operating gains rather than balance-sheet amplification.
Among firms in the same industry, those earning a high return on assets while carrying low total liabilities to assets should outperform, because their profits do not depend on financial leverage.
groups.why: Returns not leverage-driven; quality.

groups.area: Return on equity and its change
examples: Firms whose ROE has stayed above a high floor across the last three years, rather than spiking in a single year, are structurally profitable and earn higher subsequent returns.
Return on equity matters most among cheap stocks, where a high book return that the market ignores (book-to-market above 0.5) signals mispricing that corrects over the next year.
groups.why: High ROE among cheap stocks; discount plus quality.

groups.area: Return on invested capital on a liquid base
examples: Firms whose worst recent return on invested capital is still high, and which keep a large current-asset share, show a durable earnings floor that the market underprices.
Stable, high industry-relative return on capital, combined with a current-asset-heavy balance sheet, identifies firms whose profitability is durable rather than cyclical or accounting-driven.
groups.why: Durable high return on capital; quality.

examples: Seasonal winners that were long-term losers over years 2 to 5 are underpriced because investors extrapolate past underperformance and ignore a recurring calendar pattern.
Return seasonality is strongest among low-volatility stocks, where a calendar-based pattern is less likely to be swamped by idiosyncratic noise and where arbitrage against it is more costly.
groups.why: Seasonality not addressed.

examples: Stocks that enjoyed strong same-month seasonal returns while reporting high accruals, meaning earnings exceed operating cash flow, are overpriced by calendar-driven investor attention. Their seasonal premium reflects flo
groups.why: Avoids high-accrual seasonal winners; quality.

examples: Firms whose one-year sales growth jumps well beyond their own recent growth noise are under-reacted to, so the standardized growth surprise predicts positive next-month returns.
A sales jump accompanied by slower receivables build is genuine demand, whereas a jump paired with receivables inflation signals channel stuffing or lax credit terms that later reverse.
groups.why: Revenue surprise not addressed.

groups.area: Rising R&D intensity at liquid firms
examples: Accelerating R&D intensity, meaning the pace of increase is itself rising, predicts higher returns when the firm's current ratio has been stable over the past five years.
Firms that raise R&D intensity year over year earn higher subsequent returns, but only when their current ratio shows enough liquidity to fund the program without distress.
groups.why: R&D with stable liquidity; quality.

examples: Liquidity deterioration matters for returns mainly when the firm is also adding leverage, because borrowing is what forces it to rely on a shrinking liquidity buffer.
A sustained multi-year downtrend in the current ratio combined with compounding leverage growth reflects a slow-building funding squeeze that the market under-reacts to.
groups.why: Avoids rising leverage and weakening liquidity; quality.

examples: When sales are contracting, rising SG&A is a sign of management failing to cut overhead, and the market underreacts to this failure in the cross-section.
Overhead that keeps growing while sales are shrinking signals sticky costs and weak management response to demand loss, and these firms keep underperforming.
groups.why: Avoids weak overhead management; management quality.

examples: Cheap sales are more likely to be a true mispricing when the working-capital backing behind them has been stable rather than volatile.
A firm that is cheap on sales within its industry and has never had weak working-capital backing over five years is a durable, under-priced operator.
groups.why: Cheap on sales with stable backing.

examples: Sales yield is more reliable when the revenue stream itself is stable, so cheap sales from predictable firms outperform cheap sales from volatile ones.
Revenue relative to enterprise value, rather than equity value alone, is a cleaner value signal because leveraged firms' revenue is shared between debt and equity holders.
groups.why: Cheap on sales; discount to value.

examples: When the rate of accrual growth is decelerating, the earnings base is stabilizing, and high sales-yield stocks in that state should be mispriced toward the upside.
A persistent multi-year decline in accruals scaled by book equity signals a sustained shift toward cash-backed earnings, which is underpriced relative to a cheap revenue base.
groups.why: Cheap sales with improving accrual quality.

examples: Within industries, firms that generate high free cash flow relative to their market value and report earnings backed by cash rather than accruals will earn higher returns than their peers.
Cheap-within-industry firms whose gross profitability is improving year over year outperform, because the market underreacts to margin recoveries that are not yet reflected in book-to-market.
groups.why: Cheap with cash-backed earnings; discount plus quality.

examples: Within each industry, firms with a low enterprise value to EBITDA multiple and low accruals (earnings backed by operating cash flow) are undervalued relative to their earnings quality, and this combination should deliver
groups.why: Buys lowest value-quality scores; opposes discount and quality.

examples: Consistency of cash return over a five-year window indicates a stable shareholder-first policy, and the market fails to fully price the persistence of such policies.
Payout yield is valuable only when it is funded by operating cash flow, since distributions financed by debt or equity issuance are unsustainable and tend to reverse.
groups.why: Cash-funded shareholder yield; owner alignment.

examples: Firms whose short-term debt has fallen well below its five-year peak have already repaid or termed out the borrowing that once funded working capital expansion. The distance from peak therefore measures how far a firm ha
groups.why: Reduced short-term debt; quality.

examples: The fragility of working-capital funding is greatest when short-term debt is a large and rising share of total debt, because a larger proportion must be refinanced within a year.
When short-term debt rises while the cash buffer falls, the firm is drawing down liquidity to meet obligations, a sign of acute funding pressure that the market is slow to price.
groups.why: Avoids funding fragility; quality.

examples: Stocks that fell last month while trading cheap to book value rebound as the short-term price drop reverses toward the book-anchored value.
Recent losers that carry heavy debt are oversold because leveraged holders are forced sellers, so they rebound over the next year more than lightly levered losers.
groups.why: Buys oversold cheap stocks; discount.

examples: Recent winners with no accompanying change in earnings profitability give back their gains, while winners backed by a real earnings improvement do not.
Winners of last month that are also unusually volatile give back more of the gain than calm winners, because their jump is more likely to be a transient demand surge.
groups.why: Short-term reversal not addressed.

groups.area: Shrinking share count at cheap firms
examples: Share shrinkage predicts returns only when the firm is priced cheaply relative to its operating earnings, because buybacks at high valuations destroy value rather than create it.
Firms with high operating cash earnings relative to enterprise value that also cut their share count in the latest year are underpriced, and the buyback shows management is acting on that gap.
groups.why: Cheap with share shrink; discount and alignment.

examples: Size measured as a three-year average of log market value is a more stable proxy for the firm's persistent scale. Transitory price spikes at fiscal year-end should not drive the size premium.
Within each industry, the smallest firms carry higher illiquidity and distress risk, and investors demand a premium for holding them, so relatively small firms earn higher subsequent returns.
groups.why: Size not addressed.

examples: Small firms whose return on assets has been stable over five years are underpriced, because investors discount small companies for earnings volatility they do not actually exhibit.
Small firms with a cash buffer that covers at least 20 percent of current liabilities face fewer financing frictions, so the small-size premium is captured more fully in this subgroup.
groups.why: Small size with stability; tenets silent.

examples: Firms whose accrual ratio fluctuates widely over five years have less reliable earnings, and investors underprice this instability, leading to lower subsequent returns.
Accruals are most likely to reverse when they occur alongside positive sales growth, because revenue-led expansion is where aggressive recognition and receivable build-up are most common.
groups.why: Avoids unreliable accruals; quality.

examples: Firms whose cash return on assets is high and has been steady over five years have earnings that are backed by cash, so the market underprices their persistence.
Within each industry, firms with consistently low accruals, meaning earnings backed by cash, outperform peers whose reported profits outrun their cash generation.
groups.why: Cash-backed stable earnings; quality.

examples: Stable net margins matter most when the firm can meet short-term obligations without selling inventory, so a quick ratio above one should gate the margin-stability signal.
Firms whose operating return changes little from year to year and that carry a large net current asset cushion show quality earnings that the market extrapolates too slowly.
groups.why: Stable earnings with liquidity; quality.

examples: A split is a more credible confidence signal when the firm also generates strong operating cash flow, since splitting while cash-poor could reflect price-chasing rather than fundamental optimism.

Firms with a history of splits over the past five years and strong cash flow on assets form a composite of management confidence and cash generation, and this combination earns excess returns over the following year.
groups.why: Splits not addressed.

examples: Steady earnings growth paired with low realized volatility indicates a stable, predictable business that investors discount too little, producing a mispricing that persists.
A streak of rising earnings yield (ib scaled by market value) signals that investors are underpricing a persistent improvement in profitability relative to what the stock costs.
groups.why: Earnings streak with cheapness; quality.

examples: When reported earnings rise in more years than operating cash flow does, the earnings gains are accrual-driven and less persistent, so these firms should underperform.
groups.why: Avoids accrual-driven earnings gains; quality.

examples: Heavy capital spending by firms that report essentially no R&D signals a pure bet on physical capacity with no offsetting intangible pipeline, and these firms underperform.
Firms that are rapidly adding to their existing physical base and also tilt their reinvestment toward capex are overbuilding, and the overbuilt capacity depresses future returns on capital.
groups.why: Avoids overbuilding; capital discipline.

examples: Within an industry, firms whose tax burden is growing faster than their peers are those whose earnings quality is improving relative to competitors, which should earn a return premium.
Firms whose tax burden has risen in many of the last five years show a persistent pattern of growing taxable income, which is less likely to reflect temporary accounting gains that reverse.
groups.why: Rising taxes signal earnings quality.

examples: Within an industry, firms paying more tax per dollar of equity market value are more profitable relative to their peers and are priced as cheap on a hard-to-manipulate earnings base.
A high tax yield on a firm whose revenue is growing indicates a cheap company whose earnings base is expanding, so the price has not yet caught up with the growing tax-paying capacity.
groups.why: Taxes relative to price; cheap on hard earnings.

examples: Cash-flow yield at current market value predicts returns only among firms with positive accounting earnings, where cash generation is not a distress artifact.
Firms that trade at low prices relative to their sales, while their sales are growing, are undervalued on top-line momentum that the market has not yet priced in.
groups.why: Cheap on cash flow and sales; discount.

examples: Within each industry, firms whose reported earnings exceed operating cash flow by a large amount relative to their current market value are overpriced, because accruals-driven earnings are over-extrapolated by investors
groups.why: Avoids accrual-inflated earnings priced richly.

examples: Within each industry, book-to-market predicts returns only for firms with positive current earnings. Among profitable firms, the cheapest relative to industry peers should earn the highest subsequent returns.

Value pays most when earnings have been positive for several consecutive years, which signals a durable business rather than a temporary earnings trough. A single profitable year can still reflect a value trap.
groups.why: Cheap profitable firms; discount plus quality.

examples: Momentum scaled by trailing volatility, combined with earnings yield, identifies firms whose price trend is strong relative to their own risk and whose earnings are cheap relative to price.
Value measured on three-year average book equity, rather than the latest book value, is a more stable mispricing signal that combines with momentum into a persistent expected-return ranking.
groups.why: Earnings cheapness with momentum; partial discount.

groups.area: Value with a low bankruptcy-score risk
examples: Cheap stocks earn a value premium only when they are currently pre-tax profitable; unprofitable cheap stocks are distressed and should not be bought.
Within each industry, high book-to-market firms whose retained-earnings base has never dipped over the past five years are compensated value, not distressed stocks.
groups.why: Cheap profitable with stable retained earnings.

examples: Smooth, industry-relative momentum is more persistent when the winning firm also has positive clean profitability, since price trends backed by earnings are less likely to reverse.
Volatility-scaled momentum earns its premium mainly among firms with moderate leverage, because highly levered winners carry distress and crash risk that offsets the trend premium.
groups.why: Momentum buying contradicts discount approach.

examples: When most of a stock's 12-1 gain came in the early part of the window (months t-11 to t-6) rather than the recent half, the trend has already matured, while stocks whose gains were concentrated in the most recent months
groups.why: Momentum timing avoidance not addressed.

examples: Relative price winners within an industry continue to outperform only when their real top line is also expanding; price gains without sales growth tend to mean-revert as valuations overshoot.

Industry-relative momentum is only reliable for firms that are currently profitable. Loss-making winners often rally on sentiment or takeover speculation and then fade, so the gate removes those cases.
groups.why: Momentum winners contradict discount orientation.

examples: Stocks whose industry-relative 6-month trend is strong but which dipped relative to their industry last month continue to outperform, because the short-term relative dip is a transient reversal inside a persistent relati
groups.why: Relative trend winners; not value-based.

examples: Only large industry-relative monthly moves reverse; moderate relative moves carry information and do not revert.
An industry-relative price move that is not supported by current operating cash generation reverts, whereas moves backed by cash flow tend to persist.
groups.why: Reversal timing not addressed.

examples: Working-capital expansion is most dangerous when current liabilities already consume most current assets, leaving little slack to absorb the build.
A working-capital build that recurs over three years, not a one-off, signals persistent operating stress when cash is thin relative to current liabilities.
groups.why: Avoids working-capital stress; quality.

examples: The gap between receivables plus inventory and payables, scaled by sales, measures the cash the operating cycle locks up, and firms with a larger gap relative to peers earn lower returns.
A firm sitting at the high end of its own five-year range of working-capital intensity is in a period of operating strain relative to its normal efficiency, which predicts underperformance.
groups.why: Avoids operating strain; quality.

philosophy: Oakmark Fund (Harris Associates), from oakmark.com/who-we-are: We seek to invest in businesses that are priced at substantial discounts to our estimate of intrinsic value. Analysts set a buy target at a significant discount to our estimate of intrinsic value; a sell target is set, typically at 90 to 100 percent of intrinsic value. Ideas must meet our management and business quality criteria. We view every stock purchase as if we are buying a piece of a business, and seek to invest with management teams that are well-aligned with shareholders. We are patient investors who believe that the intrinsic value of an underlying business will be recognized by the market; when we find investments that meet our criteria, we invest as owners.
